Your Project Description (max 2000 chara: Foto Recipe is an intelligence system that is inspired by what my Fujifilm X-S20 actually does when it adds film simulation. Instead of writing about the "intelligence" behind it, I built a working version of an extractive logic. Upload a photo and it reads it the way the camera would: a 5-zone tone curve (blacks, shadows, midtones, highlights, whites), real white balance/temperature, exposure, contrast, dynamic range, and grain, all pulled from the actual pixels, no presets. From that, it generates three things: a "developed pattern," an abstract, textile-looking pattern built from the photo's own real colors and tones, so it's basically a visual fingerprint of the image; a vintage-style recipe receipt that translates the readout into plain language plus the full technical settings; and a recipe chart with a pie chart of the tone zones and sliding gauges for saturation and warm/cool temp. The whole site is styled like an old-school desktop: beveled windows, pixel cursor, draggable pop-ups, so the camera's invisible math feels tactile instead of hidden in a menu. You can save recipes to 'the collection' and pull them back up later with the original photo, pattern, and receipt all together. Basically: making the camera show its work.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
keep me company. runs on the logic ELIZA used in 1966: classify what comes in, match it to a scripted line, nothing more. Borrowed directly: input is sorted into a handful of categories, each mapped to a pool of pre-written responses, the way ELIZA matched keywords to transformation rules. 
What's added: no parsing of meaning at all, and a hidden mood value — continuous, cumulative, quietly decaying — that ELIZA never had, giving the page something closer to a memory. The question underneath it: if something responds to everything you do, every time, without ever understanding any of it, is that companionship — or a very convincing imitation of one?
What did you learn from making this? (ma: This project taught me that the illusion of intelligence doesn't require intelligence at all. Before this, whenever I imagined building something that felt responsive or alive, I reached straight for a large language model — I'd never seriously considered any other way to fake understanding. Working within ELIZA's constraints forced me to think differently: keyword matching, weighted randomness, and a simple decaying mood value turned out to be enough to make a response feel personal. I learned that presence is often mistaken for comprehension, and that limitation, not complexity, is what makes a system's behavior feel intentional and alive.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
“Are You Human Enough?” is an interactive CAPTCHA project that explores how digital systems represent and classify human behavior. The project contains three versions of the same verification experience. V1 makes the mechanism visible through mouse tracking, activity logs, risk scoring, and behavioral feedback. V2 hides most of this information and presents a quieter interface, asking users to trust an unseen system. V3 sits between them: it observes typing behavior and offers short comments without revealing the complete formula.
By comparing these interfaces, the project investigates how visual design and feedback influence people’s perception of technological intelligence. The system does not truly understand whether someone is human. It translates actions—such as speed, accuracy, cursor movement, and corrections—into data and applies predefined rules. The interactive homepage connects the three experiments through draggable CAPTCHA images that move, collide, resize, and transform.

What did you learn from making this? (ma:
I learned that an interface strongly affects how intelligent, trustworthy, or threatening a system appears. Even when different versions use similar rule-based logic, exposing tracking data makes the system feel more invasive, while hiding the mechanism can make it seem smoother but also more mysterious.
Building the project also showed me that behavioral data is never neutral. A fast response, limited mouse movement, keyboard navigation, or repeated correction can be interpreted as suspicious even when it comes from a real person. These classifications depend on assumptions about what “normal” human behavior should look like.
Technically, I learned how to collect interaction data locally, visualize mouse movement, create explainable scoring rules, manage responsive interfaces, and design playful drag-and-collision interactions. Most importantly, I learned that systems do not simply recognize users—they construct representations of them from incomplete traces.
